intro: A child in Kenya sleeps under a treated net. A grandmother in Okinawa tends her garden at ninety-five. A teenager in Chicago walks past three fast-food places on the way home. Each scene is part of global health: the study of what makes people sick or well across the whole world, and what can be done about it.

In this unit you will look at two big kinds of disease. Infectious diseases, such as malaria, TB, HIV, cholera, measles and polio, are caused by germs and spread between people. Chronic diseases, such as heart disease, stroke, cancer and diabetes, grow slowly and are shaped by daily habits and surroundings. For both, you will see that money, geography and culture matter as much as medicine.

By the end, you will be able to explain how several major diseases spread and how they are prevented or treated. You will compare the roles of global health groups, read health data, and weigh evidence about diet and lifestyle. You will also be able to argue, with facts, about what does the most good for the most people.
bigQuestion: What does it take to help people everywhere live longer, healthier lives?

timeline.t: John Snow traces a London cholera outbreak to the Broad Street water pump.
Robert Koch identifies the bacterium that causes tuberculosis.
Ronald Ross shows that mosquitoes carry the malaria parasite.
The World Health Organization is founded, and the Framingham Heart Study begins.
Jonas Salk's polio vaccine is declared safe and effective.
Ancel Keys begins the Seven Countries Study of diet and heart disease.
The U.S. Surgeon General reports that smoking causes lung cancer in men.
Tu Youyou's team isolates artemisinin from sweet wormwood.
Smallpox is declared eradicated, the first human disease wiped out.
Combination antiretroviral therapy transforms HIV treatment.
The Global Fund is created to fight AIDS, TB and malaria.
The WHO recommends the first malaria vaccine for young children.

words.d: a living thing, such as a mosquito, that carries a disease from one host to another
when a germ or insect is no longer harmed by a chemical or drug that used to work
a daily combination of medicines that keeps HIV from multiplying
safe ways of removing human waste, such as toilets and sewers
protection for a whole community when enough people are immune that a germ cannot spread
wiping out a disease everywhere in the world permanently
the conditions where people live, learn and work that shape their health
an illness that lasts a long time and usually develops slowly
anything that raises the chance of getting a disease
blood pressure that stays too high over time
testing people without symptoms to find a disease early
the stores, restaurants, prices and advertising that surround a person

test.q: What carries the malaria parasite from person to person?
test.why: Female Anopheles mosquitoes pass the Plasmodium parasite between people.

test.q: Artemisinin was found by testing a plant named in which kind of source?
test.why: Tu Youyou's team drew on a text by Ge Hong from Chinese medicine.

choices: Through the air when a person with active TB coughs
test.why: TB bacteria travel in droplets when someone with active lung TB coughs.

test.q: Why was John Snow's 1854 map important?
choices: It showed cholera came from bad air
It found the first malaria parasite
It linked cholera deaths to one water pump
test.why: Snow's map showed deaths clustered around the Broad Street pump.

test.q: Which is true of antiretroviral therapy for HIV?
choices: Taken daily, it keeps the virus down and lets people live long lives
It is a vaccine for babies
test.why: ART holds HIV down when taken daily; it is not a cure.

test.q: Which disease has been eradicated worldwide?
test.why: Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980; polio and Guinea worm are close but not yet gone.

test.q: What is the main work of Gavi?
choices: Helping low-income countries buy and deliver vaccines
test.why: Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, helps poorer countries get vaccines.

test.q: Which is an example of a social determinant of health?
choices: Access to clean water and housing
test.why: Social determinants include income, housing, schooling and clean water.

test.q: What is the leading cause of death worldwide?
test.why: WHO estimates rank ischemic heart disease as the top cause of death.
Most people with high blood pressure feel fine, so it must be measured.

test.q: What was the main finding of the 1964 Surgeon General's report?
choices: Cigarette smoking causes lung cancer in men
test.why: The report concluded that cigarette smoking causes lung cancer in men.

test.q: What does hara hachi bu teach?
choices: Stop eating when about 80 percent full
test.why: The Okinawan saying means eating until about eight parts out of ten full.

test.q: Why do experts sometimes disagree about screening tests?
choices: They must weigh early detection against false positives and other harms
test.why: Screening brings benefits and harms, so experts weigh them differently.

choices: Small population-wide changes prevent many cases, though each person sees little benefit
test.why: Geoffrey Rose described how community-wide prevention helps many while each person notices little.

test.q: How are malaria in Africa and heart disease in Finland alike in the unit?
choices: Both were cured by one pill
Both were reduced by community-wide prevention, not only treatment
test.why: Bed nets and North Karelia's community changes both show prevention at work.

write.prompt: If a country had money for only one new health program, should it spend it on preventing disease or on treating people who are already sick? Choose a side, cite two or three facts or sources from this unit, and explain your claim.
tips: Name your sources, such as the WHO, UNAIDS, or the North Karelia Project.
Use at least one example of an infectious disease and one of a chronic disease.
Give the other side fairly before you explain why you still hold your view.
Use unit terms like prevention, risk factor and social determinants of health.
